newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ Treasury growth forecasts seen as optimistic.
newsitem.headline: NZ Treasury growth forecasts seen as optimistic.

text.p: New Zealand's Treasury on Thursday painted a bright economic picture of steady growth and rising budget surpluses just a month before a general election, but economists said the projections may be optimistic.

Treasury forecast growth of 2.5 percent in the year to March 1997. For the 1997/98 year it projected growth of 3.7 percent, underpinned by a second round of tax cuts which take effect on July 1, 1997.

"The growth forecasts, I think, particularly for 96/97, are a bit on the optimistic side relative to where we see things going, and I think most others as well," said ANZ chief economist Paul Stewart.
"They've revised them down slightly, but we would have expected them to come down a bit more."
In its previous forecasts prepared for the budget in May, the government said GDP would rise 2.6 percent in 1996/97 and four percent in 1997/98.

Finance Minister Bill Birch said fresh projections showed the government would have a 1996/97 budget surplus of NZ$2.866 billion, or 3.1 percent of GDP. In the May budget the government forecast a surplus of $2.758 billion or 2.9 percent of GDP.
Surpluses were forecast to rise thereafter to $6.4 billion by 2000, while unemployment, now 6.2 percent, was seen nudging up to 6.3 percent by March 1997 before falling back slightly.
"I think the numbers actually look a little bit better than what I was envisioning," said SBC Warburg economist Robin Clements.
"I think the macro growth and unemployment do look a tinge on the optimistic side, but even if you do crank their numbers back to consensus, it really doesn't make an awful lot of difference."
Economists agreed that the government had scored important political points with the protrayal of a healthy economy.

"Basically the robust picture that you had in May is still intact," Clements said. "In terms of the big picture, you've got big solid surpluses and debt being repaid at a rate of knots. It keeps your options open for spending or tax cuts in the future."
Treasury said that signs of abating inflationary pressures would allow monetary conditions to ease gradually from the December 1996 quarter, which economists said mirrored the market's expectations.
Net public debt as a percentage of GDP would fall to 27.6 percent by June 1997 from the current 32.5 percent and Treasury forecast it would shrink to 13.3 percent by 2000.
Bankers Trust chief economist David Plank said the Treasury had traditionally been more bullish in its economic outlook than other forecasters, but its track record has been good.
"The Treasury has always had a stronger view of the economy than virtually any other forecaster, and on average over the last five years they've been proved right," he said.
"We'll know in about a year or 18 months' time whether they've been proved right again. The contrast with the Reserve Bank's numbers tomorrow is going to be pretty interesting."
The central bank will release its economic projections on Friday. -- Wellington Newsroom (64 4) 4734746
